extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Plato/Republic; undergraduates and general readers of classical philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts Plato’s prescriptive criteria for selecting and educating rulers (the philosopher‑king) as discussed in the Republic: curriculum order, personal qualifications, stages/ages of training, duties and cautions. Useful for understanding Platonic pedagogy and political prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory descent of philosophers into the world
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘They must be forced down again among the captives in the den to partake of their labours and honours.’ For the good of the State, philosophers who reach the light must return to rule and serve rather than remain in contemplation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulers must not remain aloof in philosophical contemplation; those trained as rulers are to take turns governing and learn to ‘use your eyes in the dark’ (practical experience). Anti‑pattern: allowing philosophic elites to seclude themselves and refuse civic duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of the State: service for the common good
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Our purpose in framing the State was not that our citizens should do what they like, but that they should serve the State for the common good of all.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political and educational arrangements should subordinate individual preference to the common good. This principle justifies compulsory duties for philosophic rulers and citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary branches of early education: gymnastic and music
rubrics_metrics.description: Early education has two branches, gymnastic (occupied with the body) and music (the sister art, which infused a natural harmony into mind and literature); neither alone suffices to produce rulers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical training and literary/cultural formation are foundational but must be followed by higher studies. Anti‑pattern: relying only on bodily or literary training for leadership formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary science for intellectual ascent: number (calculation)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Nothing remains to us but that universal or primary science of which all the arts and sciences are partakers, I mean number or calculation.’ Number is a conductor to thought and being; arithmetic sharpens the wits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arithmetic/number theory is prized not for practical counting alone but as an intellectual training that stimulates abstraction and the ability to distinguish and relate. Mathematic study must be pursued in the spirit of philosophy, not shopkeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometry (plane → solids → solids in motion) as second stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometry should ‘elevate the soul’ and assist in contemplation of the idea of good; the order proposed is plane geometry, then geometry of solids, then solids in motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometry is to be studied abstractly (to the idea), not instrumentally for technical arts. Anti‑pattern: treating geometry merely as practical craft or tactical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astronomy as study of solids in motion (third stage) — problem‑centred
rubrics_metrics.description: Astronomy (the motion of solids) draws the soul upwards only when placed on a scientific, problem‑based footing; mere star‑gazing is criticized as ‘looking up at the ceiling.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize abstract, problem‑driven astronomy (mathematical dynamics) rather than empirical or observational truisms when using it pedagogically toward dialectic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonics/music as abstract science related to the good
rubrics_metrics.description: Harmonics are to be investigated abstractly (Pythagorean approach) and related to the idea of good; mere empiricists who test intervals by ear miss the higher import.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study music/theory as a discipline of proportions and relations that trains the intellect; avoid purely audiological, empirical, or craft‑oriented approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical sciences are prelude to dialectic, not substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: All these mathematical sciences are ‘only the prelude’; they sharpen and elevate but are not dialectic itself. The mathematician’s faculty is distinct from the higher philosophical sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, harmonics to prepare the mind for dialectic; do not mistake mathematical skill for the ability to reason from first principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialectic as the capstone science
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialectic is ‘that science which defines and explains the essence or being of each nature,’ converts the soul out of opinion into intellect, and is ‘the coping‑stone of the sciences.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialectic is the final training that teaches to ask and answer the ultimate questions and to grasp the idea of the good. Entry to dialectic is conditional on prior mathematical discipline. Anti‑pattern: exposing novices to dialectic before sufficient preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal selection criteria for rulers (qualities required)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulers (disciples) ‘must be constant and valiant, good‑looking, and of noble manners,’ and must have natural ability improvable by education: quick at learning, capable of mental toil, retentive, solid, diligent, combining intellectual with moral virtues; not lame, one‑sided, or ‘a maimed soul.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection favors balanced, robust bodies and minds, temperate character, and demonstrable intellectual and moral potential. Anti‑patterns include physical or mental one‑sidedness, feebleness, or moral instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age‑staged selection and training timetable
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational stages and selections: initial playful learning in youth; at twenty select promising disciples to relate sciences; at thirty make a further selection for abstraction and dialectic; then commence advanced training (suggested ‘six, or perhaps five years’), followed by about fifteen years of practical service in the world, and at fifty return to contemplation and possibly rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training is phased: childhood/youth for basics and discovery of bent; early adult selections (20, 30) for deeper study; a long period of practical experience; culminating return to leadership. Avoid starting dialectic too early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: do not teach dialectic too early to the young
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Let us take every possible care that young persons do not study philosophy too early.’ Young learners are like puppies who play with arguments, become unsettled, and may end in hypocrisy or roguery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay serious dialectical instruction until maturity (around thirty) to prevent youthful skepticism and instability. Anti‑pattern: exposing impressionable youth to abstruse dialectic leading to paradoxical contrarianism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity that rulers be unwilling leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘For those who rule must not be those who are desirous to rule; and, if you can offer to our citizens a better life than that of rulers generally is, there will be a chance that the rich... may bear rule.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideal rulers should rule out of duty, not ambition; the polity should make ruling comparatively unattractive in worldly terms to ensure virtuous motives. Anti‑pattern: rewarding ambition with honors that attract the wrong natures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political and educational institutional measures (communal arrangements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Features of the perfect State include commoning of wives and children among guardians, common living for soldiers (receiving no pay, only food), and removal of citizens over ten years of age to expedite education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional design is part of forming the guardian class: communal provisions and early separation of children are used to shape loyalties and education. These are normative prescriptions for the ideal polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two disorders of eyesight to avoid in rulers and statesmen
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato distinguishes two pathological outlooks: (1) the theorist intoxicated with general maxims and remote ideas (sees everything at false distances), and (2) the narrow professional/tradesman who sees only immediate, local interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training and selection should aim to balance broad, principled sight with practical competence; avoid extremes of utopian abstraction and parochial narrowness in those entrusted with high office.
